moments.title: A network overview
moments.text: The video introduces graph theory through networks.

moments.title: Vertices and edges
moments.text: Identify vertices, edges and degree in the illustrated graph.

moments.title: Directed and undirected
moments.text: Arrows affect which direction an edge may be traversed.

moments.title: Weighted and unweighted
moments.text: A weight can represent a cost or time rather than a count.

moments.title: Subgraphs and routes
moments.text: The presenter names route types but refers learners elsewhere for their definitions.

moments.title: Adjacency tables
moments.text: The video introduces tables and matrices for direct connections.

moments.title: Rows are from, columns are to
moments.text: The illustrated table uses the starting vertex for the row and the ending vertex for the column.

moments.title: From table to matrix
moments.text: The presenter enters the one-step adjacency matrix.

moments.title: Two-step walks
moments.text: A matrix square counts two-step connections; repeated vertices or edges are allowed in a walk.

moments.title: Three-step walks
moments.text: The cube counts three-step walks under the same adjacency convention.

moments.title: Minimum spanning trees
moments.text: The overview turns to connecting vertices at minimum weight.

moments.title: Edge and vertex routes
moments.text: The video introduces postman and travelling-salesman contexts; see the correction.

moments.title: Review
moments.text: The video closes with an overview and practice recommendation.

notes.title: Transition matrices need further study
notes.text: The video illustrates adjacency matrices and powers but does not construct a transition matrix or develop all walk-counting cases. These are explained on this page.
notes.write: Distinguish the adjacency count, an edge weight and a transition probability.

notes.title: Routing statement later in the video
notes.text: A shortest closed Chinese postman route covers every edge at least once and may repeat edges; it is not always possible to traverse each edge exactly once.
notes.write: Matrix powers count walks, not necessarily paths or optimal routes.

ican.text: I can construct an adjacency matrix for a directed or undirected graph using a stated row–column convention.
I can use matrix powers to count walks of exactly $k$ edges and sums of powers for a range of lengths.
I can distinguish a walk count from a weighted adjacency table or shortest-path calculation.
I can construct a transition matrix from a graph and a stated probability rule.
I can interpret a matrix entry and check the convention, direction and treatment of zero-step walks.

ku.text: Fix an order of vertices and a convention before constructing a matrix. Here $A_{ij}$ is the number of directed edges from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$; for a simple graph it is $0$ or $1$. An undirected simple graph gives a symmetric matrix.

Under this row-from, column-to convention, the $(i,j)$ entry of $A^k$ is the number of walks of exactly $k$ edges from $i$ to $j$. A walk may repeat vertices and edges. For a directed graph, every step must follow the arrow.
The entry of $A^2$ is $(A^2)_{ij}=\sum_h A_{ih}A_{hj}$. Each term counts choices of a first step from $i$ to $h$ followed by a step from $h$ to $j$. This extends to higher powers.

For walks of lengths from $1$ through $k$, use $A+A^2+\cdots+A^k$. If zero-step walks are included, add $I=A^0$: there is one zero-step walk from each vertex to itself and none between distinct vertices.

A weighted adjacency table records the specified weight for each direct edge, such as time or cost. A dash can denote no edge. A zero weight is not automatically the same as no edge if zero-cost edges are allowed.

Ordinary powers of a weighted matrix do not generally give shortest travel costs. Matrix multiplication combines entries by multiplication and addition; shortest-route calculations require a different operation or algorithm.

A transition matrix requires a probability model. With equally likely outgoing edges, divide each edge count by the out-degree of its source. Other probability rules must be specified rather than inferred from arbitrary cost weights.

For column probability vectors, define $P_{ij}=P(\text{next}=i\mid\text{current}=j)$. Each column sums to one and $\mathbf p_{n+1}=P\mathbf p_n$. This is the transpose orientation of the row-from adjacency matrix used above.

If a source has no outgoing edges, an equal-outgoing transition rule cannot be applied without an additional convention. Strong connectivity guarantees a positive out-degree for each vertex in a nontrivial directed graph.
When counting paths, trails or shortest routes, do not substitute a walk count without checking the additional restrictions. Matrix powers count all walks of the specified length.

misc.better: It counts walks of exactly three edges. Add powers for a range of lengths.

misc.better: Walks may repeat vertices and edges unless a question imposes additional restrictions.

misc.weak: A cost-weighted adjacency matrix squared gives shortest two-edge costs.
misc.better: Ordinary matrix multiplication does not implement shortest-path minimisation.
A directed graph generally produces a nonsymmetric matrix under a fixed ordering.

misc.weak: Normalize arbitrary travel costs to obtain movement probabilities without any assumption.
misc.better: A probability rule must be given. Equal outgoing choices are one possible model, not an automatic consequence of costs.

misc.weak: Add $I$ to count only walks that actually move.
misc.better: $I$ counts zero-step walks. Include it only when length zero is allowed.

terms.text: A matrix recording direct connections under a specified vertex order and row–column convention.
A sequence of adjacent vertices and traversed edges; vertices and edges may repeat.
The number of edges traversed, counting repeated traversals.
A table recording an edge’s specified weight rather than just the existence or count of a connection.
A matrix of one-step movement probabilities under a specified orientation and probability rule.
A walk that stays at its starting vertex and traverses no edges.

formula.text: Under the row-from adjacency convention, $(A^k)_{ij}$ counts walks of exactly $k$ edges from $i$ to $j$.
For column probability vectors, $P_{ij}=P(\text{next}=i\mid\text{current}=j)$ and $\mathbf p_{n+1}=P\mathbf p_n$.

worked.prompt: A directed network has vertices $A,B,C$ and arcs $A\to B$, $A\to C$, $B\to C$, $C\to A$ and $C\to B$. Their respective travel times are $2,5,3,4,1$ minutes. Use vertex order $A,B,C$.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Construct the unweighted adjacency matrix using rows as starting vertices and columns as destinations.
parts.a: $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\0&0&1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}$. For example, $A_{AC}=1$ because there is an arc from $A$ to $C$, while $A_{BA}=0$.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find $A^2$ and interpret its entry in row $A$, column $C$.
parts.a: $A^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&1&0\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}$. The entry $(A^2)_{AC}=1$ counts one walk of exactly two arcs from $A$ to $C$: $A\to B\to C$.

parts.label: c
parts.q: How many walks of one, two or three arcs go from $A$ to $C$?
parts.a: The corresponding entries of $A$, $A^2$ and $A^3$ are $1,1,2$. Therefore $(A+A^2+A^3)_{AC}=4$. The three-step walks are $A\to C\to A\to C$ and $A\to C\to B\to C$.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Write the weighted adjacency table as a matrix, using a dash for no direct arc.
parts.a: With rows from and columns to, the direct travel-time table is $\begin{pmatrix}-&2&5\\-&-&3\\4&1&-\end{pmatrix}$ minutes. These are edge weights, not walk counts or transition probabilities.

parts.label: e
parts.q: At each vertex, suppose each outgoing arc is equally likely. Construct a column-stochastic transition matrix and find the distribution after two steps from $A$.
parts.a: The out-degrees are $2,1,2$. With columns as current vertices and rows as next vertices, $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1/2\\1/2&0&1/2\\1/2&1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Each column sums to $1$. From $\mathbf p_0=(1,0,0)^T$, $P^2\mathbf p_0=(1/4,1/4,1/2)^T$.

kq.q: Why does a matrix power count walks?
kq.model: Each multiplication sums over possible intermediate vertices. Products count ways to combine consecutive edges, and the sum collects all such choices.

kq.q: Why does a walk count not give a path count automatically?
kq.model: A walk may repeat vertices and edges; a path has additional restrictions. Matrix powers include repeated-route cases.

kq.q: Why does the transition matrix here have columns summing to one?
kq.model: Each column represents a current vertex, and the probabilities of its possible next vertices sum to one. A row-stochastic convention is also possible if used consistently.

kq.q: Why can a weighted table not be normalized into probabilities without context?
kq.model: Weights such as travel time express costs, not likelihoods. The problem must specify how choices depend on them.
